summary: Provides guidance on collaboration between the ITU-T and the Internet Engineering Task Force on developing standards. It updates and obsoletes RFC 3356. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Two big clubs both make rules for the internet. This memo explains how they should work together and not step on each other's toes.

questions: how do ietf and itu-t collaborate
what is the ietf new-work mailing list
subtitle: How the IETF and the ITU-T keep each other informed, share documents and avoid duplicate work.

tldr.problem: The IETF and the ITU-T both write standards that touch IP, but they organize their work very differently, so overlap and surprises are easy.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC gives non-normative guidance: name contact points, watch each other's new-work mailing lists, use liaison statements for formal communication, and cross-reference documents instead of writing joint text.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational RFC that obsoletes RFC 3356 and is updated by RFC 9141. It carries no protocol and no direct security implications.

today: RFC 6756 is an Informational RFC, not a standard, and it is updated by RFC 9141. It obsoleted RFC 3356.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
This document provides non-normative guidance on collaboration between the Telecommunication Standardization Sector of the International Telecommunication Union (ITU-T) and the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF). Its stated aim is early identification of topics of mutual interest, so that the two organizations can work constructively and with mutual respect.

The two sides are organized differently. In the IETF, work is done in working groups, mostly on open public mailing lists, and working groups are grouped into areas managed by area directors. In the ITU-T, work is defined by study Questions, mostly worked on in meetings led by rapporteurs. Questions sit in working parties, which report to a study group (SG).

Because of this, the RFC recommends establishing contact points early. The natural pairings are an ITU-T study group chairman with an IETF area director, and an ITU-T rapporteur with an IETF working group chair.
sections.eli5: One club has teams with team captains and the other has teams with coaches. Before they play together, each team should know who to call on the other side.

sections.title: Staying Informed About Each Other's Work
sections.content:
Each side is responsible for watching the other. ITU-T study groups should review IETF working group charters and active Internet-Drafts, and if they find common ground, the study group leadership should contact both the IETF working group chair and the responsible area director(s). A formal liaison statement may accompany that contact. The IETF, in turn, reviews each study group's list of Questions and work programme from time to time.

For proposed new work, the IETF forwards all draft charters for new and revised working groups, and all Birds-of-a-Feather (BOF) session announcements, to the IETF new-work mailing list. An ITU-T mailing list, maintained by the Telecommunication Standardization Bureau (TSB), is subscribed to it, and study group leadership may subscribe to that list. Going the other way, study groups send updates to the new-work list when Questions are first drafted or created, or when their terms of reference are drafted or updated.

The RFC warns that the IETF turnaround time for new working group charters can be as short as two weeks, so the list should be monitored consistently. Study group chairmen can comment on a charter by writing to the IESG mailing list and stating their ITU-T position and the nature of their concern.
sections.eli5: Each club keeps an eye on the other's bulletin board, and there is a shared mailing list where new projects are announced. Charters can move fast, so someone has to read the list regularly.

sections.title: Representation and Formal Communication
sections.content:
ISOC, including the IETF, is a Sector Member of the ITU-T, so ISOC delegates have the same rights as other Sector Members. Experts chosen by IETF leadership normally take part in ITU-T meetings as ISOC delegates. In the other direction, a study group chairman can authorize members to attend an IETF meeting as official ITU-T delegates, and under IETF process their opinions get equal weight with those of any other working group participant.

Informal communication between experts is encouraged. Formal communication from an ITU-T study group, working party or rapporteur group to an IETF contact point must be explicitly approved and identified as coming from that body. Formal liaison statements follow the procedures in RFC 4053, and the IETF posts the ITU-T statements it receives on a liaison statements web page, with a named person responsible for each.

Both sides run mailing lists. In the IETF the mailing list is the primary vehicle for discussion and decision-making, and working group lists are open to all subscribers. ITU-T lists are formal lists set up by the TSB, and individual subscribers must be affiliated with an ITU-T member or associate, though the ISOC focal point can help IETF experts get access.
sections.eli5: Visitors from one club can come to the other's meetings, and what they say counts just like anyone else's. Official letters between the clubs have to be clearly marked as official.

sections.title: Sharing Documents Without Merging Them
sections.content:
Working drafts are shared by email, by pointing to a URL, or by attaching them to a formal liaison statement. The RFC discourages attachments in proprietary formats on IETF mailing lists, and notes that the official versions of all IETF documents are in ASCII.

IETF documents usually reach the ITU-T as liaison statements, or exceptionally as a contribution from ISOC. The IETF working group must agree the drafts are of mutual interest, and the area directors must approve before the TSB circulates them. ITU-T texts can go to the IETF as liaison statements or as Internet-Drafts, which the RFC notes expire six months after publication. Text submitted this way is governed by the IPR rules in RFCs 5378, 3979 and 4879.

The envisaged outcome of collaboration is that one body documents the work in full and the other references it. Common or joint text is discouraged because the two organizations approve and revise documents differently. Recommendation ITU-T A.5 describes how Recommendations reference other organizations' documents, and Section 6.1.1 of RFC 2026 covers referencing open standards in RFCs.
sections.eli5: When both clubs care about the same topic, one of them writes the rulebook and the other just points to it, instead of both writing one together.

sections.title: Changes Since RFC 3356 and Security
sections.content:
This document obsoletes RFC 3356 and is based on text from RFCs 2436 and 3356. The Abstract notes that the bulk of it is common text with ITU-T A Series Supplement 3 (07/2012), approved by the ITU-T's TSAG on 4 July 2012.

The changes include merging the introduction into the scope section, adding information on copyright and IPR, updating liaison manager authorization and formal liaison statement transmission to current IETF procedures, and adding a description of preliminary efforts: ITU-T focus groups and IETF BOF sessions. Focus group participation is not limited to ITU-T members, and IETF participants from a country that is a member of ITU-T can take part fully. Obsolete URLs were also refreshed.

The Security Considerations section is a single sentence: documents that describe cooperation procedures have no direct Internet security implications.
sections.eli5: This is the updated version of an older memo. It fixes old addresses, adds how to start talking before a project officially begins, and says nothing here can hurt your computer.

cells: Long-term positions of several years, giving stable contacts for a topic.
Working positions of a year or more that end with the topic, so contact gets the work done.
